title: Παῖς καὶ λέων ⟨γεγραμμένος⟩
titleEn: The Boy and the Painted Lion
part: The Boy and the Painted Lion (Chambry 295 · Perry 363)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 295 (= Perry 363). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Υἱόν τις μονογενῆ γέρων δειλὸς ἔχων γενναῖον καὶ κυνηγεῖν ἐφιέμενον, τοῦτον καθ’ ὕπνους εἶδεν ὑπὸ λέοντος θανατωθέντα.
sentences.tr: Huion tis monogenē gerōn deilos echōn gennaion kai kynēgein ephiemenon, touton kath’ hypnous eiden hypo leontos thanatōthenta.
sentences.l: A certain timid old man, having an only son, high-spirited and set on hunting, saw this son in his sleep put to death by a lion.
sentences.i: A timid old man had an only son, high-spirited and eager for the hunt, and he saw the boy in his sleep killed by a lion.
sentences.n: The accusative Υἱόν is set out in front and then taken up again by τοῦτον — a way of naming the person the sentence is about before saying anything about him. ἐφίεμαι with the infinitive is to set one's heart on doing a thing. After a verb of seeing, θανατωθέντα is a supplementary participle: he saw him as killed, not merely saw him. καθ’ ὕπνους is 'in sleep', the regular phrase for a dream.

sentences.t: Φοβηθεὶς δὲ μὴ ὕπαρ γένηται καὶ ἀληθεύσῃ ὁ ὄνειρος, οἴκημα κάλλιστον καὶ μετέωρον κατασκευάσας, ἐκεῖσε τὸν υἱὸν παρεφύλαττε.
sentences.tr: Phobētheis de mē hypar genētai kai alētheusēi ho oneiros, oikēma kalliston kai meteōron kataskeuasas, ekeise ton huion parephylatte.
sentences.l: And fearing lest it become waking fact and the dream prove true, having built a chamber, very fine and high up, he kept his son guarded there.
sentences.i: Fearing that the dream might pass over into waking and come true, he built a splendid chamber high above the ground and kept his son under watch there.
sentences.n: ὕπαρ is the waking reality set against ὄναρ, the dream: the old man's fear is precisely that the dream will cross over into daylight. φοβηθείς μή with the subjunctive is the clause of fearing. ἐκεῖσε is 'thither', a word of motion used loosely here with a verb of keeping still.

sentences.t: Ἐζωγράφησε δὲ καὶ τὸ οἴκημα πρὸς τέρψιν παντοίοις ζῴοις, ἐν οἷς καὶ λέων ἐμορφώθη.
sentences.tr: Ezōgraphēse de kai to oikēma pros terpsin pantoiois zōiois, en hois kai leōn emorphōthē.
sentences.l: And he painted the chamber too, for delight, with animals of every kind, among which a lion also was figured.
sentences.n: ζωγραφέω is literally to write living things, the ordinary word for painting from life. ἐμορφώθη, 'was given shape', keeps the lion at one remove: it is a form on a wall, and the fable will not let the reader forget it.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ταῦτα μᾶλλον ὁρῶν πλείω τὴν λύπην εἶχε.
sentences.tr: Ho de tauta mallon horōn pleiō tēn lypēn eiche.
sentences.l: But he, seeing these all the more, had the greater grief.
sentences.i: But the more the son looked at them, the more his grief grew.
sentences.n: Ὁ δέ marks the change of subject: it is the son who is meant here, not the father, who held the last three verbs.

sentences.t: Καὶ δήποτε πλησίον τοῦ λέοντος στάς· « Ὦ κάκιστον θηρίον, εἶπε, διὰ σὲ καὶ τὸν ψεύστην ὄνειρον τοῦ ἐμοῦ πατρὸς γυναικείᾳ ἐνεκλείσθην φρουρᾷ· τί σοι ποιήσω ; »
sentences.tr: Kai dēpote plēsion tou leontos stas· « Ō kakiston thērion, eipe, dia se kai ton pseustēn oneiron tou emou patros gynaikeiāi enekleisthēn phrourāi· ti soi poiēsō ; »
sentences.l: And once, standing near the lion: « O foulest of beasts, he said, because of you and my father's lying dream I was shut up under a womanish guard; what am I to do to you? »
sentences.i: And one day he stood beside the lion: « You vilest of brutes, he said, it is for you and for my father's lying dream that I am penned up like a woman; what shall I do to you? »
sentences.n: γυναικείᾳ φρουρᾷ is a guard-post fit for a woman — the insult is to be kept indoors while other young men hunt. τί σοι ποιήσω is the deliberative question, 'what am I to do to you?'. The space before the Greek question mark is Chambry's house punctuation and is kept in the Greek; English takes none.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἰπὼν ἐπέβαλε τὴν χεῖρα τῷ τοίχῳ ὡς τυφλώσων τὸν λέοντα.
sentences.tr: Kai eipōn epebale tēn cheira tōi toichōi hōs typhlōsōn ton leonta.
sentences.l: And having said this he flung his hand against the wall, as one about to blind the lion.
sentences.n: ἐπιβάλλω τὴν χεῖρα with the dative is to throw the hand upon a thing; the violence of it is what the next sentence turns on. ὡς with a future participle gives the purpose as the doer conceives it — 'intending to blind'. It is one of the standard ways Greek says why an action is done.

sentences.t: Σκόλοψ δὲ τῷ ὄνυχι αὐτοῦ ὑπεισδὺς ἄλγημα ὀξὺ καὶ φλεγμονὴν μέχρι βουβώνων εἰργάσατο· πυρετός τε ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀνάψας τὸν παῖδα θᾶττον τοῦ βίου ὑπεξήγαγεν.
sentences.tr: Skolops de tōi onychi autou hypeisdys algēma oxy kai phlegmonēn mechri boubōnōn eirgasato· pyretos te epi toutois anapsas ton paida thatton tou biou hypexēgagen.
sentences.l: But a splinter, having slipped in under his nail, worked a sharp pain and an inflammation as far as the groin; and a fever, blazing up on top of this, carried the boy out of life all too soon.
sentences.i: But a splinter ran in under his nail and set up a sharp pain and a swelling that spread as far as the groin; and on top of that a fever caught light and carried the boy out of life before his time.
sentences.n: σκόλοψ is a splinter or thorn; ὑπεισδύς, 'having slipped in underneath', is the root-aorist participle of ὑπεισδύω. βουβών is the groin, where the swelling of the glands showed how far the infection had run. ἀνάψας is transitive in form, 'having kindled', but stands here intransitively of the fever itself catching light. τοῦ βίου is a genitive of separation with ὑπεξήγαγεν, which is to lead a man quietly out from under a thing.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων καίπερ γραπτὸς ὢν τοῦτον ἀνῃρήκει, μηδὲν τῷ τοῦ πατρὸς ὠφεληθέντα σοφίσματι.
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn kaiper graptos ōn touton anēirēkei, mēden tōi tou patros ōphelēthenta sophismati.
sentences.l: And the lion, though he was a painted one, had killed him, helped in nothing by his father's contrivance.
sentences.n: καίπερ with the participle is concessive, 'though he was'. ἀνῃρήκει is pluperfect: by the close the deed already stands done. σόφισμα is a clever device — the father's cunning is exactly what fails, and the participle ὠφεληθέντα, accusative and agreeing with τοῦτον, says so.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἃ δὴ μέλλει συμβαίνειν τινί, ἐγκαρτερείτω τούτοις γενναίως καὶ μὴ σοφιζέσθω· οὐ γὰρ ἐκφεύξεται.
sentences.tr: Hoti ha dē mellei symbainein tini, enkartereitō toutois gennaiōs kai mē sophizesthō· ou gar ekpheuxetai.
sentences.l: That as for the things which are going to befall a man, let him bear up under them bravely and not play the clever man; for he will not escape.
sentences.i: The story shows that a man should bear up bravely under whatever is going to befall him, and not try to be clever about it; for he will not escape.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἐγκαρτερέω with the dative is to hold out patiently in a thing, to endure it — not to fight it off. ἐγκαρτερείτω and σοφιζέσθω are third-person imperatives, 'let him…', and they take up the relative clause ἃ δὴ μέλλει συμβαίνειν through the dative τούτοις.
